'''Karl Hermann Amandus Schwarz''' ({{IPA|de|ˈhɛʁman ˈʃvaʁts|lang}}; 25 January 1843 – 30 November 1921) was a [[Germans|German]] [[mathematician]], known for his work in [[complex analysis]].

==Life==
Schwarz was born in [[Sobieszów|Hermsdorf]], [[Austrian Silesia|Silesia]] (now [[Sobieszów]], [[Poland]]). In 1868 he married Marie Kummer,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Carathéodory |first1=C |title=Hermann Amandus Schwarz |journal=Deutsches biographisches Jahrbuch |date=1921 |volume=III |issue=6 |pages=236–238 |doi=10.1002/zamm.19210010615 |bibcode=1921ZaMM....1..494M |url=https://archive.org/details/DeutschesBiographischesJahrbuchBd031921/page/n233/ |access-date=7 July 2021}}</ref> who was the daughter to the mathematician [[Ernst Eduard Kummer]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bENTBQAAQBAJ|title=Creators of Mathematical and Computational Sciences|last1=Agarwal|first1=Ravi|last2=Sen|first2=Syamal|date=11 November 2014|publisher=Springer|isbn=9783319108704|pages=297–298|language=en}}</ref> and  Ottilie née Mendelssohn (a daughter of [[:de:Nathan Mendelssohn (Instrumentenbauer)|Nathan Mendelssohn]] and granddaughter of [[Moses Mendelssohn]]). Schwarz and Kummer  had six children, including his daughter Emily Schwarz.<ref name=":0" />

Schwarz originally studied [[chemistry]] in Berlin but Ernst Eduard Kummer and  [[Karl Weierstrass|Karl Theodor Wilhelm Weierstrass]] persuaded him to change to [[mathematics]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://www-gap.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~history/Biographies/Schwarz.html|title=Schwarz biography|last1=O'Connor|first1=J. J.|last2=Robertson|first2=E. F.|website=www-gap.dcs.st-and.ac.uk|publisher=The MacTutor History of Mathematics|access-date=22 May 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160605014322/http://www-gap.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~history/Biographies/Schwarz.html|archive-date=5 June 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>  He received his Ph.D. from the Universität Berlin in 1864 and was advised by Kummer and Weierstrass.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=7487|title=The Mathematics Genealogy Project – Hermann Schwarz|website=www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu|access-date=22 May 2016|archive-date=7 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200207011442/https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=7487|url-status=live}}</ref> Between 1867 and 1869 he worked at the [[University of Halle]], then at the [[ETH Zurich|Swiss Federal Polytechnic]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4siw31DPONUC|title=Academic Genealogy of Mathematicians|last=Chang|first=Sooyoung|date=1 January 2011|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=9789814282291|pages=77–78|language=en}}</ref> From 1875 he worked at [[Göttingen University]],<ref name=":1" /> dealing with the subjects of [[complex analysis]], [[differential geometry]] and the [[calculus of variations]]. He died in [[Berlin]] on 30 November 1921.

==Work==
Schwarz's works include ''Bestimmung einer speziellen Minimalfläche'', which was crowned by the Berlin Academy in 1867 and printed in 1871, and ''Gesammelte mathematische Abhandlungen'' (1890).

Among other things, Schwarz improved the proof of the [[Riemann mapping theorem]],<ref>{{Cite arXiv|last=Bottazzini|first=Umberto|author-link=Umberto Bottazzini|date=30 April 2003|title=Algebraic truths vs geometric fantasies: Weierstrass' Response to Riemann|eprint=math/0305022}}</ref> developed a special case of the [[Cauchy–Schwarz inequality]], and gave a proof that the ball [[isoperimetric inequality|has less surface area]] than any other body of equal volume.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Schwarz|first=Hermann Amandus|date=1884|title=Proof of the theorem that the ball has less surface area than any other body of the same volume|journal=News of the Royal Society of Sciences and the Georg-August-Universität Göttingen|volume=1884|pages=1–13}}</ref> His work on the latter allowed [[Émile Picard]] to show solutions of differential equations exist (the [[Picard–Lindelöf theorem]]).<ref name=":3" />

In 1892 he became a member of the [[Berlin]] [[Academy of Science]] and a professor at the [[University of Berlin]], where his students included [[Lipót Fejér]], [[Paul Koebe]] and [[Ernst Zermelo]]. In total, he advised at least 22 Ph.&thinsp;D students.<ref name=":2" /> In 1914 Schwarz's friends and former students published a volume with 34 articles in celebration of the 50th anniversary of his doctoral dissertation.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1916-02811-4|title=Book Review: ''Mathematische Abhandlungen, Hermann Amandus Schwarz zu seinem fünfzigjährigen Doktorjubiläum am 6. August 1914 gewidmet von Freunden und Schülern''|year=1916|last1=Gronwall|first1=T. H.|author-link=Thomas Hakon Grönwall|journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society|volume=22|issue=8|pages=406–408|doi-access=free}}</ref>

His name is attached to many ideas in mathematics,<ref name=":0" /> including the following:
